title: How Ice Ages Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how ice ages work, starting with casual banter about avocado toast, gut flora and the weather. They cover the current Quaternary ice age and its interglacial periods, the Wisconsin glaciation, and early folk recognition of glacier evidence in the Alps. They discuss Louis Agassiz's ice age hypothesis, James Hutton's ideas on gradual change, and glacial erratics. They describe glacier size and weight, glacial till, loess deposits, and the albedo feedback loop. They cover Milutin Milankovitch's orbital cycles, ice core air bubbles, and competing causes such as Himalayan uplift, weathering and CO2 drawdown, dust and volcanoes, and sunspots tied to the Little Ice Age. They close with human-caused climate change, possible future glaciation, and effects on human evolution. A listener mail segment covers the origin of English meat names (Norman French vs. Germanic words). The episode ends with a sign-off.

segments.title: Sponsor read and opening banter
segments.summary: A Squarespace sponsor read, then the hosts open with chatter about avocado toast, gut flora and the late-summer weather.

segments.title: Ice age basics and the Holocene
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Earth is in an ice age during an interglacial period of the Quaternary glaciation, and distinguish glacial from interglacial periods and stadials from interstadials. They describe the Wisconsin glaciation in North America.

segments.title: Greenhouse, icehouse and snowball Earth
segments.summary: Discussion of three climate settings of Earth's history: greenhouse, icehouse and snowball, drawing on a New Scientist article.

segments.title: Early recognition of glaciers and erratic boulders
segments.summary: Early folk explanations for displaced boulders, Swiss and German peasants noticing receding glaciers, Louis Agassiz's first ice age hypothesis and its reception, and James Hutton's idea of gradual change in Earth's past.

segments.title: Glacial erratics and evidence of glaciers
segments.summary: Erratics are heavy boulders moved far from their origin by glaciers, with examples in the Swiss Alps and Central Park. U-shaped valleys, grooves and scrubbed rock are also evidence. Ice thickness of about a mile is noted.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break in the episode.

segments.title: Extent and weight of the last ice age
segments.summary: The last glaciation covered about a third of Earth, with ice reaching across North America and Europe. Ice weight and lower sea levels are discussed, plus the hosts' anecdotes about skating on frozen ponds. Glacial till and polished bedrock are also covered.

segments.title: Loess, cooling and the albedo feedback
segments.summary: Loess dust deposits from glacial grinding are described, and the hosts explain that a roughly 10 degree Fahrenheit drop was enough. Glacier growth depends on cooler summers and less melt, and albedo reflection creates a compounding feedback.

segments.title: Milankovitch cycles and ice core evidence
segments.summary: Milutin Milankovic's orbital calculations of Earth's tilt, wobble and orbit, and the 41,000 and 100,000 year cycles found in ice core air bubbles.

segments.title: Causes of ice ages: tectonics, CO2, dust, sunspots
segments.summary: Competing theories: plate tectonics and mountain uplift such as the Himalayas, weathering that draws CO2 from the air, volcanic and atmospheric dust, and sunspot cycles linked to the Little Ice Age by E. W. Maunder.

segments.title: Future ice age and human influence
segments.summary: Debate over whether another ice age is coming, a study on sunspots that the media overstated, the effect of human-caused warming, and ice ages possibly shaping human evolution, brain growth and sewing.

segments.title: Listener mail: English meat names
segments.summary: Matt Gallaford of Bristol explains that Norman French words like mutton and beef came from the upper-class gentry, while peasants kept Germanic words like sheep and cow.

segments.title: Outro and contact info
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give social media and website contact information.
